script.opening: “Thanks for taking this. I didn’t know who else to go to. It’s not about a patient — it’s about Richard. I think he’s been drinking. Before work. And I don’t want to get him into trouble, so I need this to stay between us. Can it?”

facts.text: If asked for specifics: “Three mornings this month — the 2nd, the 9th and the 14th — I smelled alcohol when he came in at half eight. Not last night’s, fresh. On the 9th after lunch his words were a bit slurred and he was flushed. He keeps mints in his drawer now.”

Only if asked about today or whether he is in work now: “This morning. Same smell. He’s in his room doing paperwork now. He’s doing the minor ops list at two — six patients — and he’s on call till half six.”

If asked about any clinical concerns: “Last week the pharmacist rang about a warfarin prescription — he’d written 10 mg instead of 1 mg. It was caught. It’s been logged as a significant event but nobody connected it.” She has also noticed he is “behind with results, snappy, forgetting things”.
“His wife left him in July. He’s living on his own. He’s lost weight.” He drives to work.

Only if asked how Richard seems in himself or whether she is worried about him as a person: “Last week he said, ‘Sometimes I wonder what the point of any of it is.’ He laughed it off. I haven’t stopped thinking about it.”
If asked: “I think Pam on reception has noticed. I’ve been moving some of his patients to other clinicians quietly.” She has not spoken to Richard, the practice manager or other partners.
If asked how she is: “He’s my line manager. He signs off my hours. I’ve worked here fifteen years. If this goes wrong… And I should have said something weeks ago.”
“I want him to be OK. I want patients to be safe. I don’t want to be the one who ended his career.”

Anxious, loyal, slightly tearful; keeps checking “this stays between us?”. If the doctor promises complete confidentiality, look relieved — but if the doctor then does nothing about today’s list, stay uneasy. If the doctor says “I’ll have to report him to the GMC”, panic: “No — that’s exactly what I didn’t want.” If the doctor explains that patient safety comes first, that Richard will be approached supportively, and that she will be protected, agree: “OK. If it’s done kindly.” Reveal the “what’s the point” comment only if asked about Richard as a person. Reveal today’s smell and the 2 pm list only if asked about today.

ice.ideas: “He’s drinking because his wife left. He needs help, not punishment.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — Richard said “sometimes I wonder what the point of any of it is”, and she is frightened he may harm himself; she also feels guilty for not speaking sooner and fears consequences for her job because he is her line manager. She shares the comment only if asked about Richard as a person, and her own fears only if asked how she is.
ice.expectations: That the candidate will sort it out quietly without anyone knowing it came from her.

cues: “I need this to stay between us. Can it?” — confidentiality that cannot be promised where patients are at risk.
“He’s in his room now” (if asked about today) — an immediate patient-safety issue this afternoon.
“I want him to be OK” — concern for a colleague’s wellbeing, opening the door to his risk.

checkpoints.text: Thanks her, takes the concern seriously, and is honest early that complete confidentiality cannot be promised if patients may be at risk — while explaining her concern will be handled carefully and supportively
Establishes specific facts: dates and observations, whether today, his clinical duties this afternoon (minor surgery, on call), the warfarin error, other performance changes, who else knows
Asks about Richard as a person — life events, mood, and the “what’s the point” comment — recognising possible risk to his own safety

Acts on the immediate risk today: arranges a private conversation with Richard before 14:00 with another partner or the practice manager; if impaired or he does not deny it, he does not see patients; the list and on-call are covered; he does not drive home
Approaches Richard supportively, and responds to possible suicidal thoughts (asks directly, does not leave him alone if at risk, involves his GP, crisis support or NHS Practitioner Health)

Plans proportionate escalation in line with GMC Good medical practice 2024: inform the practice’s clinical lead/partners; seek advice from the NHS England responsible officer (performers list); occupational health; NHS Practitioner Health and LMC support for Richard; GMC referral if concerns are not addressed or patients remain at risk; link the warfarin significant event
Documents factual observations and actions (date, time, what was seen, what was done) and asks Bernie to write a factual account; explains the practice’s raising-concerns / Freedom to Speak Up route
Supports Bernie: acknowledges loyalty and fear, reassures that raising a concern was right and she will not be penalised, removes the burden of covering for him, and agrees to update her

worked.txt: “Thank you for coming to me — I know that wasn’t easy. I want to be honest from the start: if patients might be at risk, I can’t promise this stays between us. But I can promise it will be handled carefully and kindly, and that you won’t be left exposed.”
“Can you tell me exactly what you’ve noticed, and when? … And today — has anything happened this morning? What is he doing this afternoon?”

“Then the first thing is this afternoon. I’ll ask our practice manager to join me and we’ll speak to Richard privately before two. If he’s been drinking, he won’t do the list or the on-call — we’ll cover it — and we’ll make sure he gets home safely without driving.”

“How does Richard seem in himself? … That comment worries me too. I’ll ask him directly how he’s feeling, including whether he’s had thoughts of harming himself, and make sure he isn’t left on his own if he is.”

“After today this needs the right support, not a cover-up: the partners need to know, we’ll take advice from the responsible officer, and there’s a confidential service for doctors — NHS Practitioner Health. Going to the GMC is for if the risk isn’t being managed — it isn’t where we start.”

“You’ve done exactly what you should. Please stop moving his patients yourself — that’s not yours to carry. Could you write down the dates and what you saw, just facts? I’ll let you know what happens.”

f.learning: A concern that a colleague is impaired is a patient-safety issue first and a welfare issue at the same time. GMC Good medical practice (2024) requires doctors to act promptly when patient safety may be compromised — it overrides personal and professional loyalty — and to support colleagues. Deal with today first (a private, supportive conversation before the next clinical session; stand him down if impaired; get him home safely), recognise that doctors with alcohol problems and life crises are at increased risk of suicide, then escalate proportionately within the practice and to the responsible officer, while signposting confidential help (NHS Practitioner Health, LMC, occupational health). Never promise confidentiality you cannot keep, document facts, and protect the person who raised the concern.

knowledge.guideline: Sources: GMC Good medical practice (2024) · GMC Raising and acting on concerns about patient safety (2012) · NHS England Framework for managing performer concerns and The National Health Service (Performers Lists) (England) Regulations 2013 · Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 · NHS Practitioner Health (self-referral service for doctors) · BMA / LMC guidance on supporting colleagues with health problems · National Guardian’s Office Freedom to Speak Up guidance
knowledge.summary: A nurse reports fresh alcohol on a GP partner’s breath before clinics, a dosing error and a worrying comment. Protect today’s patients, look after him, escalate supportively, document, and protect her.

points.t: Repeated smell of alcohol before clinics, slurred speech, a serious prescribing error, falling behind and personality change are reasonable grounds for concern — proof is not required to act.
Impairment now with clinical work imminent (minor surgery, on-call), intention to drive, or any suggestion of suicidal thoughts. Act the same day.

Good medical practice (2024): take prompt action if patient safety, dignity or comfort is or may be seriously compromised; this duty overrides personal and professional loyalties. Support colleagues who are struggling, and do not treat colleagues inappropriately or ignore poor practice.

Speak to the doctor privately with a second senior person; explain what has been observed; if impaired, he must not see patients; arrange cover; ensure safe transport home; check his wellbeing and suicide risk; do not leave him alone if at risk.

Inform the partners/clinical lead and practice manager. GP concerns are handled through the NHS England responsible officer and the performers list process — seek advice early. Occupational health assessment. GMC referral (or advice from the GMC employer liaison adviser) if the concern is serious, unresolved, or patients remain at risk.

NHS Practitioner Health (confidential, self-referral service for doctors with mental health and addiction problems), his own GP, LMC pastoral support, BMA wellbeing support, Sick Doctors Trust. Doctors have higher suicide rates than the general population, particularly with alcohol misuse and relationship breakdown.

points.h: Protecting the person who raises it
points.t: Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 protects workers who raise concerns in good faith from detriment. Use the practice’s raising-concerns/Freedom to Speak Up policy; she should not be left covering for him.
Contemporaneous factual notes: dates, times, observations, who was present, actions taken and advice sought. Link the warfarin significant event to the review.

model.text: Hi Bernie, thanks for messaging. Are you somewhere private? Take your time.
It’s about Richard. I think he’s been drinking before work. I don’t want to get him into trouble — can this stay between us?

Thank you for coming to me — that took courage. I’ll be honest: if patients might be at risk, I can’t promise it stays between us. But I promise it’ll be handled carefully and kindly, and you won’t be left exposed. Can you tell me what you’ve noticed?
Three mornings this month I smelled fresh alcohol — the 2nd, 9th and 14th. On the 9th he was slurring after lunch. And the warfarin error last week.
That’s really clear, thank you. What about today — has anything happened this morning, and what is he doing this afternoon?
Same smell this morning. He’s doing the minor ops list at two and he’s on call till half six.
And does anyone else know? Have you noticed anything else — results, memory, mood?
Pam on reception, maybe. He’s behind, snappy. I’ve been moving some of his patients quietly.
How does Richard seem in himself, with everything that’s happened?
model.why: Invites the hidden concern about his wellbeing

model.text: His wife left in July. Last week he said “sometimes I wonder what the point of any of it is.” He laughed it off.
That worries me too. I’ll ask him directly how he’s feeling, including whether he’s had thoughts of harming himself, and make sure he isn’t left alone if he’s at risk.
model.why: Recognises and plans for suicide risk

model.text: So the first thing is this afternoon. I’ll ask the practice manager to join me and we’ll speak to Richard privately before two. If he has been drinking, he won’t do the list or the on-call — we’ll cover them — and we’ll make sure he gets home without driving.
Will you tell him it was me?
I’ll talk about what has been observed, not who observed it. He may guess — and if he reacts badly towards you, that isn’t acceptable and you’ll be protected. You did exactly the right thing.
model.why: Protects the person raising the concern

model.text: After today, it needs proper support rather than a cover-up: the partners will need to know, we’ll take advice from the NHS England responsible officer, and I’ll encourage him to contact NHS Practitioner Health — a confidential service for doctors. The GMC is for if the risk isn’t being managed, not where we start. We’ll link it to the warfarin event.
model.why: Proportionate escalation in line with GMC guidance

model.text: It will be. Please stop moving his patients yourself — that isn’t yours to carry. Could you write down the dates and what you saw, just the facts? I’m making a note of this call too. How are you doing?
model.why: Removes her burden; documentation; checks on her

model.text: Relieved. Guilty I didn’t say sooner.
You’ve said it now, and that matters. I’ll update you this afternoon.
model.why: Closes with support and a follow-up commitment

social.t: Staff raising concerns about a partner or line manager fear for their jobs; practices must make it safe to speak up.
Relationship breakdown, isolation and weight loss alongside alcohol misuse raise concern about depression and suicide.

legal.t: Protects workers who make protected disclosures from detriment or dismissal.
NHS England’s responsible officer manages concerns about GPs on the performers list and can take supportive or restrictive action.
Preventing an impaired colleague from driving protects him and the public.

professional.t: Act promptly on patient-safety concerns, support colleagues, and contribute to a culture where concerns are raised and acted on.
Start locally and supportively, escalate if the risk is not controlled; seek advice (responsible officer, GMC employer liaison adviser, defence organisation).
Keep factual, dated notes of observations, conversations and actions.

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by either colluding (“leave it with me, it stays between us”) and letting him run today’s list, or by jumping straight to a punitive GMC referral and forgetting he is a person at risk.

wordPics.clearFail: Promises secrecy and does nothing today, or goes straight to a punitive referral; no exploration of facts; ignores his wellbeing and her position.
wordPics.fail: Takes the concern seriously but misses today’s clinical risk or the suicide-risk comment, or gives a vague plan without escalation or documentation.
wordPics.pass: Establishes facts, acts on today’s risk with a private supportive conversation, plans appropriate escalation and support, documents and reassures the nurse.
wordPics.clearPass: All of the above, plus: honest about confidentiality from the start, finds and acts on the “what’s the point” comment, ensures he does not drive, uses proportionate escalation (responsible officer, Practitioner Health; GMC if unresolved), links the significant event, and protects and follows up with Bernie.
